entries.title: Pecans
entries.summary: The pecan is a hickory nut native to the Mississippi valley and the South, rich, buttery and quick to toast. New Orleans cooks put it where French recipes put almonds: in pralines, pies, crusts for fish and butter sauces.
entries.guest: Pecans are native to Louisiana, and New Orleans cooks use them where French recipes use almonds, as in the pralines on our bread pudding; on the Pecan Gulf Fish they go into the pecan bordelaise.

paras: The pecan is the nut of a tall hickory tree, Carya illinoinensis, native to the Mississippi valley, Texas and northern Mexico. It grows wild along Louisiana's rivers and in orchards across the South. The nuts ripen in autumn: the green husk splits on the tree, and from about October into December the nuts fall or are shaken down.

Inside the thin shell sit two ridged halves, sweet and buttery, softer and richer than an almond, because a pecan is roughly seven parts in ten fat. That oil carries the flavour, and it is why pecans toast fast, burn fast and go stale fast. In the Creole kitchen the pecan took the almond's place, in the praline and in butters for fish.

Buy halves for garnish and cheaper pieces for crusts, crumbles and pralines. Good pecans are plump, evenly light gold to tan, with a clean, sweet smell. Shrivelled, dark or greasy nuts are old, and a sharp smell like paint or old crayons means the oil has gone rancid: no cooking fixes that. Keep shelled pecans airtight in the fridge for a few months or in the freezer for longer, away from onions and fish, whose smells they soak up, and taste one from every new case before it goes into a dish.

Toasting drives off moisture, warms the oil and browns the surface, so the nut turns crisp and its flavour deepens. Spread the pecans in one layer on a tray and toast them at 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirring halfway, until they smell nutty and the cut faces turn a shade darker, the colour of light toffee. Halves take longer than pieces. Tip them onto a cold tray at once: the oil holds heat, and nuts left on the hot tray keep cooking.

For a handful, use a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 5 minutes, tossing all the time and never walking away. The gap between toasted and burnt is a minute or less, and burnt pecans taste bitter and acrid; one scorched batch spoils a whole sauce, so throw it out and start again. Toast on the day, cool before chopping, and salt them while still warm if the dish wants it.

Pecans run from breakfast to dessert; pralines and the pecan bordelaise have their own entries. Pecan pie is a custard of eggs, sugar, syrup and butter poured over pecans in a pastry case and baked at about 175°C (347°F) for 50 to 60 minutes, until the centre barely wobbles.

For a pecan crust on fish, pulse raw pecans with breadcrumbs: they toast in the pan, while nuts toasted in advance scorch before the fish is done. Dip the fillet in flour, egg wash and the crumb, and cook it in butter and oil over medium heat: higher, and the nuts burn before the fish cooks through. A pecan butter sauce is a cousin of meunière, fish cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley: here toasted pecans are warmed in brown butter with lemon and parsley.

The name comes from an Algonquian word for a nut, carried into English through the French pacane. The orchard pecan began in Louisiana: in 1846 or 1847 Antoine, an enslaved gardener at Oak Alley Plantation in St. James Parish, grafted wood from a tree with large, thin-shelled nuts onto other trees. His variety, later named Centennial, won a prize at the 1876 Centennial Exposition in Philadelphia, and grafting made the pecan an orchard crop.

Pecans run through four dishes at Brennan's. On the Pecan Gulf Fish they go into the pecan bordelaise; confirm at lineup which bordelaise it is before pairing a wine. On the New Orleans Bread Pudding they arrive as pralines. The Baked Apple on the Traditional Breakfast bakes under an oat and pecan crumble, and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake carries pecans for crunch. Never call our pecans Louisiana-grown until the kitchen confirms the supplier.

Say pih-KAHN, the common Louisiana way; PEE-kan is heard across the South too, so never correct a guest. Pecans are a tree nut, and they travel through crusts, butters, crumbles, pralines and sauces where a guest may not expect them, so every nut question goes to the kitchen and the service note, never a verdict from you.

cards.front: What is a pecan?
cards.back: The nut of a hickory tree native to the Mississippi valley and the South: rich, buttery and softer than an almond.

cards.front: When are pecans harvested?
cards.back: In autumn: the husks split on the tree and the nuts fall or are shaken down from about October into December.

cards.front: Why do pecans toast, burn and go stale so quickly?
cards.back: A pecan is roughly seven parts in ten fat; the oil holds heat, browns fast and turns rancid with age and warmth.

cards.front: How do you toast pecans on a tray?
cards.back: In one layer at 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes, stirred halfway, until nutty and a shade darker, then onto a cold tray.

cards.front: Can a scorched batch of pecans be saved?
cards.back: No. Burnt pecans taste bitter and acrid and spoil a whole sauce, so throw them out and toast a fresh batch.

cards.front: Why do pecans appear where French recipes use almonds?
cards.back: Louisiana cooks swapped in their native nut, which is how the praline became a pecan sweet and fish took pecan butters.

cards.front: How do you keep a pecan crust on fish from burning?
cards.back: Cook the fillet in butter and oil over medium heat; on high heat the pecans burn before the fish cooks through.

cards.front: How do you spot rancid pecans?
cards.back: A sharp smell like paint or old crayons and a bitter taste: the oil has turned, and no cooking fixes it.

cards.front: How should shelled pecans be stored?
cards.back: Airtight, in the fridge for a few months or the freezer for longer, away from onions and fish, whose smells they absorb.

cards.front: How is pecan usually said in Louisiana?
cards.back: Usually pih-KAHN; PEE-kan is heard across the South too, so a server never corrects a guest.

cards.front: Which four Brennan's dishes carry pecans?
cards.back: The Pecan Gulf Fish, the New Orleans Bread Pudding with its pralines, the Baked Apple's crumble and the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.

cards.front: A guest asks whether a dish has nuts in it. What do you do?
cards.back: Take it to the kitchen and the service note every time: pecans hide in crusts, butters and sauces, and a server never gives a verdict.

questions.q: Why do pecans burn faster than most nuts when they are toasted?
questions.answer: They are roughly seven parts in ten fat
distractors: They are dried and coated with added sugar
They are toasted in the shell
They hold more water than almonds
questions.why: The oil holds heat and browns quickly, so a pecan goes from toasted to bitter in a minute or less.

questions.q: Which method toasts pecans evenly on a tray?
questions.answer: One layer at 175°C (347°F) for 6 to 10 minutes
distractors: Piled deep at 175°C (347°F) for 20 to 25 minutes
questions.why: One layer toasts evenly and moderate heat browns the nuts without scorching their oil; stir them halfway so the edges of the tray do not burn.

questions.q: In which season are pecans harvested?
questions.answer: Autumn
questions.why: The husks split in autumn, and the nuts fall or are shaken down from about October into December.

questions.q: The French praline sugared one nut; New Orleans remade it with pecans. Which nut did the French original use?
questions.answer: The almond
questions.why: Louisiana cooks used their native pecan where France used almonds, which is how the praline became a pecan sweet.

questions.q: A tray of pecans has scorched dark brown. What should the cook do?
questions.answer: Throw them out and toast a fresh batch
distractors: Rinse them and toast them again
Use them in a sauce where nobody sees them
Salt them hard to hide the bitterness
questions.why: Burnt pecans taste bitter and acrid, and that taste carries into anything they touch; nothing hides it.

questions.q: A new case of pecans smells sharp, like paint. What does that tell you?
questions.answer: The oil has gone rancid
distractors: They were toasted at the farm
questions.why: A paint or crayon smell is rancid oil from age, warmth or air; the case goes back, because no cooking fixes it.

questions.q: Why is a pecan-crusted fillet cooked over medium heat rather than high?
questions.answer: The pecans burn before the fish cooks
distractors: Medium heat makes the crust soak up butter
High heat turns the pecans soft
The fish must steam in its own juice
questions.why: Pecans brown far faster than a fillet cooks, so moderate heat lets crust and fish finish together.

questions.q: A guest orders the pecan dish and says PEE-kan. What does the server do?
questions.answer: Carry on: both ways are heard
distractors: Explain that PEE-kan is a Northern habit
Ask the kitchen which way is right
questions.why: Louisiana mostly says pih-KAHN and PEE-kan is heard across the South, so a server never corrects a guest's way of saying it.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dish do pecans arrive as pralines?
questions.answer: New Orleans Bread Pudding
questions.why: The bread pudding carries pralines over its whiskey caramel; the fish has a pecan bordelaise, the cake pecans and the apple a crumble.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the sauce on the Pecan Gulf Fish has nuts in it. What do you do?
questions.answer: Take it to the kitchen and the service note
distractors: Offer to leave the pecans off the plate
Say the bordelaise is only garlic butter
Tell them the pecans are only a garnish
questions.why: Pecans travel through crusts, butters, crumbles and sauces, and leaving them off settles nothing; every nut question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Leidenheimer and New Orleans French bread
entries.summary: New Orleans French bread is a long loaf with a thin crust that shatters and a light, cottony crumb, softer than a Paris baguette. Leidenheimer, baking since 1896, makes the loaf most po-boys are built on.
entries.guest: The crisps on our Creole Caesar, in place of croutons, are made from Leidenheimer French bread: the city's po-boy loaf, from a family bakery founded in 1896.

paras: New Orleans French bread is the city's everyday loaf: long and slim, with a crust so thin it shatters into flakes at the first bite and a crumb so light it is almost cottony. Beside a Paris baguette it is softer, airier and less chewy, with a pale, crackly skin rather than a thick, hard crust. It is built to be split and filled: the crumb gives under fried shrimp or a ladle of gravy while the crust keeps its crackle.
That lightness has a price: the loaf stales fast. It is at its best on the day it is baked and dry by the next morning, which is why New Orleans kitchens have so many uses for yesterday's bread.

It is a lean dough of flour, water, yeast and salt, and some bakers add a little sugar or fat. A baker's working ratio for a lean French dough is about 65 parts water and 2 parts salt to 100 parts flour by weight, with 2 to 3 parts fresh yeast. Knead until smooth and stretchy, rise until doubled, about an hour, then shape long loaves and give them a second, generous rise, which builds the airy crumb. Slash the tops and bake with steam at about 230°C (446°F) for 18 to 25 minutes; the steam keeps the crust thin and lets the loaf open fully.

In a restaurant the loaf is bought, not baked. Keep it in its paper bag at room temperature, never in plastic, which softens the crust, and never in the fridge, which stales it faster. To revive a day-old loaf, pass it quickly under the tap and warm it at 180°C (356°F) for 4 to 6 minutes, then serve it at once. For bread crisps, slice thin on the bias, about 3 mm (1/8 inch), brush with butter or oil and bake at 160 to 175°C (320 to 347°F) for 8 to 12 minutes, until dry right through and golden at the edges.

The po-boy is the loaf's great use: a length of French bread split and filled with fried shrimp, fried oysters or roast beef in gravy. Ordered dressed, it carries shredded lettuce, sliced tomato, pickles and mayonnaise; plain means none of those. Drain fried fillings on a rack and dress the sandwich at the last moment, so the crumb stays crisp-edged rather than soggy.

Stale French bread is the base of two New Orleans classics with their own entries: bread pudding, the bread soaked in sweet custard and baked, and pain perdu, lost bread, slices dipped in egg and milk and fried. The light crumb drinks custard without turning to paste.

George Leidenheimer came from Deidesheim in Germany and opened his bakery on Dryades Street in 1896, baking the dense breads of home. His customers wanted the light, crisp loaf the city already loved, so he turned to French bread, and in 1904 the bakery moved to Simon Bolivar Avenue, where it still bakes. The family has run it for four generations, by the bakery's own account.

Its bread is older than the po-boy, so never say Leidenheimer invented the sandwich. The story the city tells dates the name to the streetcar strike of 1929, when Bennie and Clovis Martin, former streetcar conductors with a restaurant by the French Market, fed striking poor boys free sandwiches. Historians note the brothers may have sold the sandwich before the strike, so tell it as the city's story.

At Brennan's the loaf becomes the Leidenheimer crisps on the Creole Caesar: thin toasted slices in place of croutons, with gem lettuce, a smoked oyster dressing and Grana Padano. The menu prints the name and nothing more, so how the crisps are cut and toasted, and whether with butter or oil, is a kitchen answer, never a guess.

Say LY-den-hy-mer. Naming the bread turns a garnish into a piece of New Orleans: the crisps come from the city's po-boy bread, from a bakery founded in 1896. A guest who asks whether the bakery is still family run can be told yes: the founder's family runs it, in its fourth generation. Wheat and gluten questions about the crisps or the dressing go to the kitchen and the service note.

entries.title: Mirliton, satsuma and Creole cream cheese
entries.summary: Three foods of the New Orleans household larder: the mirliton, a pale green squash stuffed for the holidays; the satsuma, a seedless Plaquemines mandarin; and Creole cream cheese, a tangy cultured cheese eaten for breakfast. Each is rarely seen on restaurant menus.
entries.guest: Mirliton, satsumas and Creole cream cheese are New Orleans home cooking: a holiday squash, a local winter mandarin and a tangy breakfast cheese, more often met at a family table than on a menu.

paras: These three belong together because they belong to the house, not the restaurant. For generations they filled the household larder of New Orleans: a mirliton vine on the back fence, a bag of satsumas from down the river, a tub of Creole cream cheese from the corner creamery. Home cooks knew them by season; restaurant menus seldom printed them. Knowing them shows a cook what the city eats when it cooks for itself.

The mirliton is the chayote, a pale green, pear-shaped squash of the gourd family, creased at its broad end, with crisp, watery flesh, a mild taste between cucumber and courgette and one soft, flat seed. Many in the city say MEL-ih-tawn; MIR-lih-tahn is heard too. The vines fruit in autumn, which is why stuffed mirliton is a Thanksgiving and Christmas dish in New Orleans homes.

The satsuma is a seedless mandarin first grown in Japan, with a loose skin that peels in one go and sweet, juicy segments. It grows in Plaquemines Parish and across south Louisiana. Creole cream cheese is no foil-wrapped block: it is a soft, fresh farmer's cheese of skimmed milk, soured with a culture and set with a little rennet, nearer a thick yoghurt or fine ricotta, eaten with sugar and cream or fruit.

Mirlitons come in from autumn into early winter; choose firm, unblemished, pale green fruit, heavy for its size, with no soft spots or sprouting, and keep them loosely wrapped in the fridge for up to two weeks. Satsumas run roughly October to December. Choose fruit heavy for its size with snug skin; a puffy, light satsuma is past its best, and a green-tinged one may be ripe, because the skin colours late. Creole cream cheese comes fresh from a few small dairies: buy it close to its date and keep it cold.

Peel raw mirliton under running water or in gloves, because its sap leaves a sticky, tingling film on the hands. To stuff them, halve them lengthwise and simmer until a knife slides in, 30 to 45 minutes by size. Lift out the seed and scoop the flesh, leaving a shell about 6 mm (1/4 inch) thick. Chop the flesh and drain it well, then cook it down with onion, celery and green pepper sweated in butter until the water is gone. Fold in shrimp, crabmeat or diced ham with breadcrumbs to bind, fill the shells, top with crumbs and butter, and bake at 190°C (374°F) for 20 to 30 minutes until golden.

For Creole cream cheese, bring 3.8 litres (1 gallon) of pasteurised skimmed milk to room temperature, stir in 240 ml (1 cup) of cultured buttermilk and a few drops of rennet diluted in cool water, cover, and leave it at 21 to 24°C (70 to 75°F) for 12 to 24 hours, until it sets to a soft curd with clear whey at the edge. Ladle it gently into perforated moulds, drain it in the fridge for 6 to 8 hours, then keep it at 5°C (41°F) or below and use it within a week. Satsumas are best raw: segmented into salads, or juiced for vinaigrettes, glazes and a satsuma beurre blanc.

Creole cream cheese was once sold by many New Orleans dairies; as they closed through the twentieth century it nearly vanished. Around 2000 the New Orleans food writer and broadcaster Poppy Tooker, then a Slow Food leader, championed it for Slow Food's Ark of Taste, a catalogue of foods at risk of being lost, and small dairies, Mauthe's among them, began making it again. Mirlitons have had hard years too: heat and storms have killed many old backyard vines, and local growers now collect and share heirloom strains to keep them going.

None of the three is printed on our menus, so a question about them usually comes from a local with a memory or a curious cook. Meet it warmly: the mirliton is the holiday squash families stuff with shrimp and ham, the satsuma the winter mandarin from down the river, Creole cream cheese the old breakfast cheese eaten with sugar and cream. If a special uses one, learn it at lineup, and send any dairy or shellfish question about the dish to the kitchen.

entries.title: Eggs and yolks
entries.say: As it reads: eggs and yolks.
entries.summary: The hen's egg is the kitchen's binder, leavener, emulsifier and sauce base: a white of water and protein around a yolk of fat and lecithin. Freshness, grade and size decide how it poaches, peels and holds a sauce.
entries.guest: Poached on the Hussarde, soft-boiled on the Owen, and sunny side up on the breakfast hanger, with a Vital Farms pasture-raised egg. If you would like one cooked differently, I will ask the kitchen.

paras: A hen's egg is two foods in one shell. The white, about two thirds of the weight, is water and protein: it sets firm with heat, whips to a foam and lifts a bake. The yolk holds the fat, flavour and colour, and carries lecithin, a natural emulsifier that lets it hold droplets of butter or oil apart in a little water. That is why a yolk can build hollandaise, béarnaise, mayonnaise and a tartare dressing.

The egg is thus the kitchen's binder, leavener, emulsifier and sauce base: a whole egg binds a forcemeat, whipped whites lift a soufflé, a yolk holds a warm emulsion, and yolks in hot cream make a custard. A large egg weighs about 50 g (1.75 oz) out of the shell, a third of it yolk.

American eggs are graded AA, A and B on the shell, the white and the yolk, and sized by the weight of a dozen: large eggs weigh 680 g (24 oz) a dozen. A fresh egg cracked onto a plate shows a thick white standing close round a tall, domed yolk; an older egg spreads thin and flat and its yolk breaks easily.

The poaching egg must be fresh, because only a thick white gathers round the yolk in the water; a thin white feathers into rags. The egg for boiling is better a week old: as an egg ages, carbon dioxide escapes through the shell, the white's acidity falls and the membrane under the shell lets go, so it peels clean where a fresh one tears. Keep eggs at 7°C (45°F) or below.

The carton describes the hen's life, not the egg's grade. Cage-free means no cages but perhaps no outdoors; free-range means some access outside, with no set space; pasture-raised, as Vital Farms prints it, means at least 108 square feet (10 square metres) of rotated outdoor pasture a hen. Never promise a yolk colour: it changes with diet and season.

Heat sets an egg in stages: the white thickens from about 62°C (144°F), is a tender, milky solid by 65°C (149°F) and firms fully nearer 80°C (176°F); the yolk thickens from about 65°C (149°F) and is firm by about 70°C (158°F). A poached egg, cooked out of its shell in water just below a simmer for about three minutes, has a set white and a running yolk; a hard-boiled egg goes past both marks and can be grated. Frying, boiling and the omelette belong to eggs to order.

Cured, a yolk becomes a seasoning: buried in salt and sugar for a day or more, rinsed and dried at a low heat until firm enough to grate, it is egg yolk bottarga, say boh-TAR-gah, named for the salted, dried fish roe it imitates. Raw, a yolk with mustard binds a tartare dressing. Raw or lightly cooked, it is the egg the consumer advisory covers; whether a yolk comes from a pasteurised egg is the kitchen's answer, and the rest is in the entry on eggs and safety.

At Brennan's the egg is poached on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Sardou, soft-boiled on the Eggs Owen, sunny side up on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak and the Duck Confit Waffle, folded into the Crab & Corn Omelette, grated hard-boiled over the Turtle Soup, and cured as the egg yolk bottarga on the Steak Tartare Cannoli; the yolk also builds the hollandaise, béarnaise, Choron and Foyot.

The menus name Vital Farms on the breakfast hanger's egg and, on the fall sheet, on the yolk of the Steak Tartare with Rye; whose eggs go into the other plates is the chef's answer. That tartare's dressing holds egg as well, so taking the yolk off does not take egg out of the plate: send the question to the kitchen.

Say how the egg is cooked: soft poached on the Hussarde and the Sardou, and check with the kitchen before promising a firmer egg. For pasture-raised, say Vital Farms, every hen with at least 108 square feet of outdoor pasture, only of the plates that print the name. For a raw or lightly cooked egg, say the consumer advisory first and send the pasteurised question to the kitchen; egg as an allergen goes to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.front: What are the two parts of an egg, and what does each do in the kitchen?
cards.back: The white, water and protein, sets firm, whips to a foam and lifts a bake; the yolk, fat and flavour, carries lecithin, the emulsifier that holds butter or oil in a sauce.

cards.front: Name the egg's four jobs in a kitchen.
cards.back: Binder, leavener, emulsifier and sauce base: a whole egg binds a forcemeat, whipped whites lift a soufflé, a yolk holds a hollandaise, and yolks in hot cream make a custard.

cards.front: Why can a yolk hold a hollandaise, a mayonnaise or a tartare dressing together?
cards.back: Its lecithin coats each droplet of butter or oil so it cannot join the next, as long as the fat goes in slowly enough for the yolk to take it.

cards.front: How do you tell a fresh egg from an old one on the plate?
cards.back: A fresh egg's thick white stands close round a tall, domed yolk; an old egg spreads thin and flat and its yolk breaks easily.

cards.front: Why must the poaching egg be fresh?
cards.back: Only a thick, fresh white gathers round the yolk in the water; a thin, older white feathers into rags.

cards.front: Why does an older egg peel cleanly where a fresh one tears?
cards.back: As an egg ages, carbon dioxide escapes, the white's acidity falls and the membrane under the shell lets go more easily, so a week-old egg peels clean.

cards.front: What does a large egg weigh, and what is the American standard for a dozen?
cards.back: About 50 g (1.75 oz) out of the shell, roughly 33 g (1.2 oz) of white and 17 g (0.6 oz) of yolk; a dozen large eggs weigh 680 g (24 oz) in the shell.

cards.back: The white begins to thicken at about 62°C (144°F), is a tender solid by 65°C (149°F) and firms fully nearer 80°C (176°F); the yolk thickens from about 65°C (149°F) and is firm by about 70°C (158°F).

entries.title: Butter
entries.summary: Cream churned until its fat gathers: about 80 per cent fat with water and milk solids, which is why butter browns, burns and splits. The kitchen clarifies it, chills it or mounts it to suit the job, and cooks with unsalted.
entries.guest: Butter is in nearly every savoury plate we serve: it starts the pan, builds the warm sauces and finishes the rest. If you have a dairy question, I will check with the kitchen.

paras: Butter is cream churned until its fat gathers into grains and the buttermilk runs off: about 80 per cent milk fat, the American minimum, with around 16 per cent water and a little milk solids. Those two small parts explain what butter does in a pan. The water is why butter spits and foams as it melts, the foam being water boiling off at 100°C (212°F); the solids are what brown, nutty and sweet, and what burn, bitter and black, a few seconds later. Whole butter smokes at about 150°C (302°F), too low for a hard sear; clarified, with water and solids gone, it takes about 250°C (482°F).

Sweet butter, the kitchen's word for unsalted, is the cook's butter, because salt is then the cook's decision, measured at the pan; salted butter carries about 1.5 to 2 per cent salt and belongs to the bread basket. Cultured butter is churned from cream ripened with lactic cultures, as most French butter is, and tastes faintly tangy. European-style butters are churned to 82 per cent fat and above, drier and richer, which matters in pastry, where less water means a crisper layer.

Butter has four jobs on the menu. It is the fat a pan starts in, for a sweated shallot, a meunière, the Bananas Foster. It is the body of a warm emulsion, the fat that egg yolk holds in a hollandaise or béarnaise and that a reduction holds on its own in a beurre blanc. It is the gloss a sauce takes when cold butter is swirled in at the end, monter au beurre, which rounds and thickens it. And cooked until its solids toast, it is a sauce in its own right: brown butter, beurre noisette, say burr nwah-ZET.

Keep butter in three states. Cold, from the fridge at 4°C (39°F), for lamination and for beurre blanc: cold butter folded into dough stays in sheets, and cold butter whisked into a reduction melts slowly enough to be caught as an emulsion. Soft, at room temperature, for creaming with sugar and for compound butters. Clarified, melted and skimmed with the water and solids lifted away, for the high heat of a sauté and a steadier hollandaise. Butter melts at about 32 to 35°C (90 to 95°F), just below the warmth of the mouth, so it feels rich on the tongue, and a sauce mounted with it must never boil again.

In France butter draws a line across the country: the north and west, Normandy, Brittany and the Charentes, cook with butter, the south with olive oil and the south west with duck and goose fat. Brittany's butter is salted, and tradition ties that to the old salt tax, the gabelle, which Brittany did not pay under the monarchy, so salt stayed cheap there; Normandy's is sweet.

On the menu, butter is the brown butter on the Swordfish Grenobloise, stopped with acid as its solids toast nutty, and the warm brown butter vinaigrette on the Louisiana Crab Claws, the browned butter sharpened with acid and finished with fines herbes. It is the butter the frascarelli on the Chateau Espagnole are finished in, tossed until starch and fat make a glossy coat; the sheet prints only finished in butter, so anything else in that pan is the kitchen's answer.

It is the preserved lemon beurre blanc on the Redfish Véronique, cold butter whisked into a wine, vinegar and shallot reduction with no egg, and the butter melted with brown sugar into a bubbling caramel that the Bananas Foster starts in at the table.

Butter travels through more plates than a guest expects. Never answer from memory whether a plate has butter in it; whose butter the kitchen buys is not printed, and a dairy question goes to the service note and the kitchen every time. Say what butter does: brown butter is butter cooked until it tastes of hazelnuts, beurre blanc is a butter sauce without egg, and the Foster's caramel starts with butter and brown sugar in the pan.

entries.title: Cream and crème fraîche
entries.say: As it reads: cream; creme fraiche, krem FRESH.
entries.summary: Cream is the fat skimmed from milk, sold by its fat: the more fat, the better it whips, the harder it can boil and the less it splits. Crème fraîche is cream thickened and soured by cultures, and mascarpone its richer Italian cousin.
entries.guest: Crème fraîche is a cultured French cream, richer and milder than sour cream with a gentle tang, whipped on our coffee cake. If you have a dairy question, I will check with the kitchen.

paras: Cream is the fat skimmed from milk, and everything it does follows from its fat. Fat is what whips: below about 30 per cent the fat globules cannot trap air. Fat is what boils: a rich cream, low in protein, can be simmered hard and reduced without curdling. And fat resists splitting when acid or salt meets it. American labels are set by law: half-and-half at 10.5 to under 18 per cent, light cream at 18 to under 30, light whipping cream at 30 to under 36 and heavy cream at 36 and above, the cream a kitchen buys.

British labels run on the same scale with other names: single cream at about 18 per cent, whipping at 35, double at 48 and clotted at 55, so a British recipe's double cream is richer than American heavy cream and reduces faster. Any dairy question goes to the service note and the kitchen.

Crème fraîche, say krem FRESH, is cream thickened and gently soured by lactic cultures, the same kind that sour buttermilk, held warm at about 20 to 24°C (68 to 75°F) for a day until it sets. It carries at least 30 per cent fat, which is why it behaves unlike sour cream: it can be stirred into a hot sauce or simmered without splitting, and it whips. Its slightly nutty tang lifts a sweet plate and cuts a rich one. A kitchen cultures its own from heavy cream and a spoonful of buttermilk, left covered overnight.

Mascarpone, say mas-kar-POH-nay, is the Italian cousin: cream thickened with a little acid and drained rather than cultured, at about 45 per cent fat by weight, richer than heavy cream (the higher figure often quoted is of its dry matter), sweet, dense and spoonable, the body of a tiramisu. Both whip like cream, lightened with a little of it.

Cream enters a sauce in one of two ways. Reduced on its own, it is simmered in a wide pan until it has lost a third to a half and coats the back of a spoon, the nappe; it may boil, because its fat protects it, but it catches on the bottom, so swirl the pan. Stirred in off the heat, a splash softens and rounds a finished sauce. Acid and salt go in last, once the cream has reduced: lemon, wine or mustard stirred into a thin, simmering cream can grain it, and mustard boiled loses its bite.

Whipping beats air into fat. Everything cold, the cream at 4°C (39°F), the bowl and the whisk too, because cold fat globules partly join around each bubble and hold it. At soft peaks the cream holds a shape that falls over at the tip, for folding into a mousse or spooning beside a dessert; at firm peaks the tip stands, for piping. A minute past firm the cream turns grainy and then, as the fat gathers, to butter and buttermilk: there is no road back, so stop early and finish by hand.

On the menu, cream is the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin à la Moutarde, the bistro classic of shallot softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered and mustard stirred in off the heat, over a sweet tea-brined fried Cornish hen; tonight's build, the mustard included, is the kitchen's answer. It is the Creamed Spinach side: the classic build is spinach blanched, squeezed dry and chopped, bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg, but the menu prints only its name, so whether ours carries Parmesan, like the Sardou's, or flour is the kitchen's answer.

It is the whipped crème fraîche on the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, and crème fraîche is the cool, silky layer in the Steak Tartare Cannoli too. And it is the fall Chocolate Crémeux, an anglaise set with chocolate, which can set on its chocolate alone but takes a little gelatine for a firmer set; the sheet marks gelatine as present, so its source, pork, beef or fish, and a vegetarian guest's question both go to the kitchen.

Describe crème fraîche as a slightly tangy cultured cream, richer and milder than sour cream, and say krem FRESH. Call the Poussin's sauce a French mustard cream over Southern fried chicken, the whole idea of the dish. Cream hides in sauces and sides a guest may not expect, so a dairy question is never answered from memory: it goes to the service note and the kitchen.

brennans.how: The classic mustard cream sauce is shallot softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered and mustard stirred in off the heat so it keeps its bite; ours goes over the sweet tea-brined fried Cornish hen, and what goes into tonight's sauce, the mustard included, is the kitchen's answer.

Creamed Spinach, a breakfast and lunch side, prints only its name; the classic build is spinach blanched, squeezed dry, bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel and finished with Parmesan and nutmeg, and whether ours carries Parmesan or flour, and whether it is the Sardou's spinach, are the kitchen's answers.
The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake is served with whipped crème fraîche, cold cultured cream beaten to soft peaks, whose tang keeps the cake from being too sweet.

The Chocolate Crémeux is an anglaise set with chocolate, and the sheet marks gelatine, so treat it as present: whether it is pork, beef or fish, and whether the course can be made without it, are the kitchen's answers.

cards.front: How is cream sold, and why does the fat matter?
cards.back: By its fat: fat is what whips, what lets a cream boil without curdling and what resists splitting when acid or salt meets it; below about 30 per cent it cannot hold air.

cards.front: What are the American cream labels by fat?
cards.back: Half-and-half 10.5 to under 18 per cent, light cream 18 to under 30, light whipping cream 30 to under 36, heavy cream 36 and above, the one a kitchen buys.

cards.front: What are single, whipping, double and clotted cream in Britain?
cards.back: About 18, 35, 48 and 55 per cent fat; British double cream is richer than American heavy cream, so a sauce written for it reduces faster.

cards.front: What is crème fraîche, and how do you say it?
cards.back: Cream thickened and gently soured by lactic cultures, at least 30 per cent fat, richer and milder than sour cream; it can be simmered without splitting and it whips; whipped on the coffee cake, and the cool layer in the Steak Tartare Cannoli. Say krem FRESH.

cards.front: What is mascarpone, and how is it made?
cards.back: The Italian cousin, say mas-kar-POH-nay: cream thickened with a little acid and drained, at about 45 per cent fat by weight, richer than heavy cream; the 60 per cent and more often quoted is a share of its dry matter. Sweet, dense and spoonable.

cards.front: How is cream reduced for a sauce, and when do acid and salt go in?
cards.back: Simmered in a wide pan until it loses a third to a half and coats a spoon; it may boil but must be swirled. Acid and salt go in last, once it has reduced, so it stays smooth.

cards.front: Why must the cream and the bowl be cold to whip?
cards.back: Cold fat globules partly join around each air bubble and hold it; warm ones slide apart, and cream under about 30 per cent fat cannot hold air at all.

cards.front: What are soft and firm peaks for?
cards.back: Soft peaks, which fall over at the tip, for folding into a mousse or spooning beside a dessert; firm peaks, which stand, for piping.

cards.front: What happens to cream beaten past firm peaks?
cards.back: It turns grainy and then, as the fat gathers, to butter and buttermilk; there is no road back, so stop early and finish by hand.

cards.front: How is the mustard cream sauce on the Poussin made?
cards.back: In the classic way: shallot softened in butter, white wine reduced, cream simmered and mustard stirred in off the heat, because boiling dulls its bite; ours goes over sweet tea-brined fried Cornish hen, and tonight's build is the kitchen's answer.

cards.front: Why does the sheet mark gelatine on the Chocolate Crémeux?
cards.back: A crémeux, an anglaise set with chocolate, can set on its chocolate alone, but a little gelatine gives a firmer, cleaner set; the sheet marks it, so its source, pork, beef or fish, is the kitchen's answer.

cards.front: A guest asks about dairy in the Creamed Spinach: who answers, you or the kitchen?
cards.back: The service note and the kitchen, every time: cream hides in sauces and sides a guest does not expect, so it is never answered from memory.

questions.q: What is the least fat a cream needs to whip?
questions.answer: About 30 per cent
questions.why: Below about 30 per cent the fat globules cannot trap air; heavy cream, at 36 per cent and above, is what a kitchen whips.

questions.q: What is the American standard for heavy cream?
questions.answer: At least 36 per cent fat
questions.why: Heavy cream is 36 per cent and above by law; light whipping cream is 30 to under 36, light cream 18 to under 30 and half-and-half 10.5 to under 18.

questions.q: A British recipe calls for double cream. How does it differ from American heavy cream?
questions.answer: It is richer, at about 48 per cent fat
distractors: It is lighter, at about 18 per cent fat
It is the same cream under another name
It is cultured, like crème fraîche
questions.why: British double cream is about 48 per cent fat against heavy cream's 36 and above, so it whips faster and a sauce written for it reduces sooner.

questions.q: What is crème fraîche, and what thickens it?
questions.answer: Cream soured and thickened by cultures
distractors: Cream whipped with sugar until firm
Cream reduced by half over heat
Cream curdled with lemon and drained
questions.why: Lactic cultures thicken and gently sour the cream; at least 30 per cent fat, it is richer and milder than sour cream and does not split when warmed.

questions.q: When does lemon or mustard go into a cream sauce?
questions.answer: Last, once the cream has reduced
distractors: First, before the cream goes in
Halfway, while the cream is simmering
questions.why: Acid stirred into a thin, simmering cream can grain it, and mustard boiled loses its bite; once the cream has reduced its fat protects it and the sauce stays smooth.

questions.q: Why must the cream, the bowl and the whisk be cold for whipping?
questions.answer: Cold fat holds the air bubbles
distractors: Cold cream has more fat in it
Cold keeps the cream from souring
questions.why: Cold fat globules partly join around each bubble and hold it; warm ones slide apart, and the cream never thickens.

questions.q: Whipped cream has gone grainy and yellow in the bowl. What has happened?
questions.answer: It is turning to butter
distractors: The sugar went in too early
questions.why: Past firm peaks the fat gathers and the cream separates into butter and buttermilk; there is no road back, so stop early and finish by hand.

questions.q: Why does the mustard go into the Poussin's cream sauce off the heat?
questions.answer: Boiling dulls its bite and can make it bitter
distractors: Heat would curdle the cream around it
It melts into the cream only when cool
It would colour the sauce too dark
questions.why: The sauce is shallot, reduced white wine and simmered cream; mustard stirred in at the end keeps its tang, which boiling would dull.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the Chocolate Crémeux is set with gelatine and what kind. What do you say?
questions.answer: The sheet marks gelatine; its source is the kitchen's answer
distractors: It sets on chocolate alone, so there is none
It is pork gelatine, like every dessert here
It is fish gelatine, so there is no pork in it
questions.why: A crémeux can set on its chocolate alone, but the training sheet marks gelatine on ours, so treat it as present and send its source, pork, beef or fish, to the kitchen.

entries.title: Mushrooms
entries.summary: The cultivated kinds a kitchen buys, button to king oyster, and the wild ones by season; a mushroom is mostly water, so it browns only in a hot, uncrowded pan with the salt held back. Dried, pickled or preserved, it keeps its savoury depth.
entries.guest: Maggie's Mushrooms is our mushroom side, earthy and savoury; I can tell you which mushrooms the kitchen has tonight and how they are cooked, and they are a natural beside the Chateaubriand.

paras: A mushroom is the fruit of a fungus, and to a cook it is two things at once: about 90 per cent water, and a store of glutamates, the compounds behind the savoury depth, umami, of aged cheese and cured ham. Cooking drives off the water and concentrates the rest, so a handful shrinks to a spoonful that tastes of so much. White button, cremini and portobello are one species, Agaricus bisporus: the white strain sold small as the button, and the brown strain sold young as cremini and broad, dark and open-capped as portobello, deeper in flavour as it matures.

Shiitake, say shee-TAH-kee, is long grown on logs in Japan and China, meaty and smoky, with a tough stem that goes to the stockpot. Oyster mushrooms grow in soft, fan-shaped shelves and cook in moments; king oyster has a thick stem that slices into scallop-like coins. The wild kinds come by season: morels in spring, chanterelles and black trumpets through summer and autumn, cèpes, the porcini of Italy, in autumn, dear because nobody farms them. Buy them dry and firm; keep them cold in paper, never plastic, and wipe or rinse them quickly and dry them rather than soaking, since they drink water.

Three rules make mushrooms brown instead of steam. A hot pan, the fat shimmering. No crowding: a single layer, in batches if need be, because a crowded pan drops in temperature and the water the mushrooms release pools and boils them grey. And salt late: salt draws water out, so a mushroom salted at the start gives up its juice before it can colour. Leave them until golden, then toss and season. Butter burns at the heat they want, so start them in oil and add butter, garlic and herbs at the end.

What the mushrooms release is mushroom liquor, never poured away but reduced into the stock or the sauce. Duxelles, say dook-SEL, is mushrooms chopped fine and cooked slowly with shallot in butter until the pan is dry, a paste for stuffing, pastry or a sauce, named, it is said, for the Marquis d'Uxelles, whose cook was La Varenne. In a brown sauce, mushrooms sweated with shallot before the stock and wine go in give a marchand de vin its earthy base. Dried mushrooms soaked 20 to 30 minutes in warm water give a dark liquor to strain through muslin.

Preserving keeps the depth. Dried mushrooms, shiitake and cèpes above all, keep for a year in a sealed jar; pickled, cooked briefly and covered in a seasoned vinegar, they bring acid as well as savour. The kitchen's preserved shiitake on the Blackened Tofu are most likely cured in soy or pickled; what the kitchen means by preserved is the chef's answer.

The white button is the champignon de Paris, where it was first farmed at scale: tradition credits the gardeners of Louis XIV, and by the nineteenth century growers were raising it on beds of horse manure in the cool limestone quarries beneath and around the city. The Métro pushed the growers out around 1900, and the trade moved to the caves of the Loire.

On the menu, mushrooms are inside the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, a red wine and mushroom sauce in the guide's words; Brennan's own published recipe sweats mushrooms with onion, shallot and garlic, but whether tonight's sauce carries them is a question for the chef. They are the preserved shiitake on the Blackened Tofu, the earthy, meaty note against the spiced crust and the creamy rice grits.

And they are Maggie's Mushrooms, a dinner side the menu prints with no description. The likely source is Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville, upriver from Baton Rouge, run by Maggie Long and Cyrus Lester, who grow lion's mane, oyster, shiitake and chestnut mushrooms for New Orleans restaurants; the house has not confirmed that link, so say our mushroom side until the chef confirms the farm.

Learn three things at lineup for Maggie's Mushrooms: tonight's varieties, how they are cooked, and whether in butter or stock, because a guest will ask all three. Call the marchand de vin a mushroom sauce only once the chef confirms the mushrooms are in it tonight. Whether a mushroom side is vegetarian, and what the tofu's shiitake are preserved in, are kitchen answers.

faults.fault: Grey, rubbery mushrooms sitting in liquid
faults.cause: The pan was crowded or too cool, or the mushrooms were salted at the start.
faults.fix: A hot pan, a single layer in batches, and salt only once they are golden.

faults.cause: Butter alone was used at the heat mushrooms need to brown.
faults.fix: Start them in oil and add the butter, garlic and herbs at the end.

faults.cause: Sealed in plastic, where they sweat.
faults.fix: Keep them cold in paper or an open container and use them within days.

faults.fault: Grit in a sauce made with dried mushrooms
faults.cause: The soaking liquor went in unstrained.
faults.fix: Strain it through muslin and leave the last spoonful behind.

faults.fault: Browned mushrooms but a thin pan sauce
faults.cause: The mushroom liquor was poured away.
faults.fix: Keep the liquor and reduce it into the sauce.

brennans.how: The Hussarde's marchand de vin is, in the guide's words, a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, and Brennan's published recipe sweats mushrooms with onion, shallot and garlic; whether tonight's sauce carries them is a question for the chef.
The Eggs Owen carries the same marchand de vin under the short rib débris and the soft-boiled egg; confirm with the chef before promising mushrooms in it, and which kind.

A dinner side the menu prints with no description. Learn tonight's varieties, how they are cooked and whether in butter or stock at lineup, and name Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville only once the chef confirms it.

The preserved shiitake bring the earthy, meaty note that makes the Blackened Tofu satisfying against the spiced crust and creamy rice grits; most likely cured in soy or pickled, and what the kitchen means by preserved is the chef's answer.

cards.back: White button, cremini and portobello, shiitake, say shee-TAH-kee, oyster and king oyster; the wild kinds, morels, chanterelles, black trumpets and cèpes, come by season.

cards.front: Why start mushrooms in oil and add butter at the end?

cards.front: What is mushroom liquor, and what happens to it?

cards.front: Where are mushrooms inside a Brennan's sauce?

cards.back: Dried, pickled or cured in a seasoned liquid. The sheet says only preserved for the tofu's shiitake; the pack reads that as most likely a soy cure or a pickle, and what the kitchen means is the chef's answer.

cards.front: How are fresh mushrooms kept?
cards.back: Cold, dry and in paper or an open container, never sealed in plastic, where they sweat and turn slimy; buy them firm and dry, wipe or rinse them quickly rather than soak, and use them within days.

cards.front: Why is the white button called the champignon de Paris?
cards.back: Because it was first farmed on a large scale in the cool limestone quarries beneath and around Paris, on beds of horse manure, by the nineteenth century, before the trade moved to the Loire.

questions.q: Why do mushrooms shrink so much in the pan?
questions.answer: They are about 90 per cent water
distractors: Their fat renders out as they cook
Their air pockets collapse in the heat
Their sugars burn off as they brown
questions.why: A fresh mushroom is mostly water, which cooking drives off, so a handful becomes a spoonful that tastes of everything the water left behind.

questions.q: What exactly is a portobello mushroom?
questions.answer: A fully grown cremini
distractors: A wild mushroom gathered in autumn
A shiitake grown on oak logs
questions.why: White button, cremini and portobello are one species, Agaricus bisporus; the portobello is the brown strain, the cremini, grown on until its cap is broad, dark and open.

questions.q: When are mushrooms salted, and why?
questions.answer: At the end, once they are golden
distractors: At the start, so the salt cooks into them
Halfway, once they have released their liquor
Never, because salt makes them rubbery
questions.why: Salt draws water out; a mushroom salted early releases its juice into the pan and boils in it instead of colouring.

questions.q: Mushrooms are sitting grey in a pool of liquid. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The pan was crowded or too cool
distractors: They were cooked in oil, not butter
questions.why: A crowded pan drops in temperature and the water the mushrooms release pools and boils them; a hot pan, a single layer and batches let them brown.

questions.q: Why start mushrooms in oil and add the butter at the end?
questions.answer: Butter burns at the heat they need to brown
distractors: Oil makes them release more water
Butter would stop them taking salt
Oil browns them faster than any fat
questions.why: Mushrooms brown in a pan hotter than whole butter can bear; oil takes the heat, and butter, garlic and herbs go in last for flavour.

questions.q: What is duxelles, and how is it made?
questions.answer: Chopped mushrooms cooked dry with shallot in butter
distractors: A sauce of mushrooms and cream over pasta
questions.why: Finely chopped mushrooms are cooked slowly with shallot in butter until every drop of water has gone; the paste stuffs, lines pastry and deepens sauces.

questions.q: Dried cèpes have been soaked for a sauce. What happens to the soaking water?
questions.answer: Strained through muslin and added to the sauce
distractors: Poured away, because it is gritty
Used to wash the fresh mushrooms
Boiled with the stems for a stock only
questions.why: The dark liquor holds the mushrooms' flavour; it is strained through muslin to catch the grit, the last spoonful left behind, and reduced into the sauce.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the Hussarde's sauce has mushrooms in it. What do you say?
questions.answer: Confirm with the chef before promising it
distractors: Yes, it is a mushroom sauce by definition
No, marchand de vin is only wine and stock
Only on the Owen, never the Hussarde
questions.why: The guide calls the marchand de vin a red wine and mushroom sauce and Brennan's published recipe sweats mushrooms into it, but whether tonight's sauce carries them is the chef's answer.

questions.q: Before naming the farm behind Maggie's Mushrooms, what must happen?
questions.answer: The chef confirms the link
distractors: A guest says they know Maggie
The side sells out that night
questions.why: Mushroom Maggie's Farm in St Francisville is the likely source, but the house has not confirmed it, so say our mushroom side until the chef does.

questions.q: A guest asks how the shiitake on the Blackened Tofu are preserved. What do you say?
questions.answer: Ask the chef what preserved means here
distractors: They are pickled in seasoned vinegar
They are dried and soaked back
They are cured in a seasoned brine
questions.why: The sheet prints preserved and nothing more; pickling, drying and a cure are all ways to preserve a shiitake, so the chef's answer is the only one a server gives.

entries.title: Red wine in the kitchen
entries.summary: Dry red wine is a seasoning in a French kitchen: it lifts the browned bits from a pan, brings acid and tannin, and reduces into the deep sauces of the house. A sound bottle is the only kind to cook with.
entries.guest: We cook with dry red wine in sauces such as the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde; most of the alcohol cooks away but not all, so tell me if you avoid it.

paras: Red wine in a kitchen is a seasoning, not a drink. A dry red brings three things to a pan: acid, which brightens and cuts fat; tannin, the drying grip from grape skins, which gives a sauce backbone and deep colour; and fruit, which reduction concentrates into something winey and savoury. Most of the alcohol boils off, but never all of it. Deglazing, lifting the browned fond with liquid, has its own entry.

Cook with a wine you would drink: dry, sound and clean. A corked bottle, musty like a wet cellar, or an oxidised one, flat and sherry-like, cooks its fault straight into the sauce, because reduction concentrates the fault while the fruit that might have hidden it cooks off. Avoid salted cooking wine. A medium-bodied red with moderate tannin is the workhorse; a very tannic young wine reduces to bitterness, and a sweet one makes a sweet sauce. Taste the bottle before it goes near the pan.

Wine goes into a sauce before the stock, and it is reduced on its own first. Sweat shallot in butter, pour in the wine and boil it hard until it has lost at least half its volume and the raw, sharp smell of alcohol gives way to a round, fruity one. Taste it: a reduction that still bites like raw wine bites in the finished sauce; stock and butter soften it only a little. Then add the stock or demi-glace and reduce again until it coats a spoon. Reducing the wine first spares the stock an hour of boiling.

Alcohol boils at about 78°C (172°F), but it is dissolved in the liquid and leaves slowly. The USDA's table of retention factors gives about 40 per cent of the alcohol still present after 15 minutes of simmering, about 25 per cent after an hour and about 5 per cent after two and a half hours. A marchand de vin reduced for twenty minutes still carries wine.

Three classical preparations stand on red wine. Marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce, reduces red wine with shallot, or in New Orleans with onion and garlic, into brown stock. Bordelaise in its French form reduces red wine with shallot, thyme and bay into demi-glace. A daube, the Provençal braise, cooks beef slowly in red wine and stock until it falls apart; the skimmed, reduced liquid is the sauce. On this menu the house's two are the marchand de vin and the Owen's short rib braise; the pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish is most likely the New Orleans butter kind; confirm which with the kitchen.

Each wine belongs somewhere. Red goes with brown stock, beef and dark braises. Dry white goes with fish, chicken and the pale sauces, the beurre blanc above all. The fortified wines, Madeira, sherry and port, are richer and sweeter and finish a sauce rather than build it; they have their own entry. Beer stands in for wine in a Flemish carbonnade; on this menu it goes into the Shells & Cheese, whose Mimolette fondue is made with Abita Amber, and cooking leaves some of its alcohol behind.

Harsh and sour: the wine was not reduced enough before the stock went in; reduce further, or soften it with more stock and a knob of butter. Bitter and drying: too much tannin from a big young wine reduced hard; round it off with butter or a spoonful of glace. Musty or flat: the bottle was off, and no reduction cures it, so throw the sauce out.

At Brennan's two plates are built on red wine. The marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen is red wine cooked with aromatics and beef stock into a glossy brown sauce. The Owen's short rib is braised in red wine for about three hours, and its skimmed, reduced braising liquid becomes the gravy of the débris. Which wine the kitchen cooks with is not printed, so name none. Both plates carry alcohol, and their service notes say so.

At the table, call the marchand de vin the wine merchant's sauce, a red wine sauce the guide describes as red wine and mushroom; call it a mushroom sauce only once the chef confirms mushrooms are in it tonight, and say the Owen's short rib is braised in red wine. If a guest avoids alcohol, say that both plates carry wine and that cooking does not remove all of it, then offer another dish; never promise it has cooked away.

faults.fix: Reduce further; soften with a little more stock and a knob of butter.

faults.cause: A big, tannic young wine reduced hard.
faults.fix: Round it off with butter or a spoonful of glace; choose a softer wine next time.

cards.front: What does red wine do in a pan?
cards.back: Three things: its acid brightens and cuts fat, its tannin gives backbone and deep colour, and its fruit concentrates as it reduces into a winey, savoury depth.

cards.front: Which red wine should you cook with?
cards.back: One you would drink: dry, sound and clean, medium-bodied with moderate tannin. Never a corked or oxidised bottle, and never salted cooking wine.

cards.front: Why does a corked or oxidised bottle ruin a sauce?
cards.back: Reduction concentrates everything, the fault included, while the fruit that might have hidden it cooks off; no reduction cures it.

cards.front: When does the wine go in, and how far is it reduced?
cards.back: Before the stock, on its own, by half or more, until the raw smell of alcohol gives way to a round, fruity one. Taste it for rawness before the stock goes in.

cards.front: How much alcohol is left after a sauce simmers?
cards.back: The USDA's retention table gives about 40 per cent after 15 minutes, 25 per cent after an hour and 5 per cent after two and a half hours, so never promise it has all cooked away.

cards.front: Which preparations stand on red wine, and which two does the house serve?
cards.back: Marchand de vin, French bordelaise and the daube; at Brennan's, the marchand de vin on the Hussarde and the Owen and the Owen's short rib braise. In each the wine is reduced before the stock goes in.

cards.front: Where do red, white, fortified wine and beer each belong?
cards.back: Red with brown stock, beef and dark braises; dry white with fish, chicken and the pale sauces; Madeira, sherry and port to finish a sauce; beer, on this menu, in the Abita Amber fondue of the Shells & Cheese.

cards.front: A finished red wine sauce tastes harsh and sour. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.back: The wine was not reduced enough before the stock went in. Reduce further, or soften it with a little more stock and a knob of butter.

cards.front: A red wine sauce is bitter and drying on the tongue. Why?
cards.back: Too much tannin, from a big young wine reduced hard. Round it off with butter or glace, and choose a softer wine next time.

cards.front: Where does red wine appear at Brennan's, and what does a server say?
cards.back: In the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and Eggs Owen, and in the red wine braise of the Owen's short rib. Both plates carry alcohol; the wine is not printed, so name none.

questions.q: Which bottle belongs in the pan for a marchand de vin?
questions.answer: A dry, sound red you would drink
distractors: A corked bottle, since cooking hides the fault
A sweet red, for a rounder sauce
questions.why: Reduction concentrates a fault and cooks off the fruit that might hide it; cooking wine carries salt, and a sweet wine makes a sweet sauce.

questions.q: When does the red wine go into a sauce, and how far is it reduced?
questions.answer: Before the stock, by half or more
distractors: After the stock, with no reduction
At the very end, off the heat
With the butter, as the sauce is mounted
questions.why: Reducing the wine on its own drives off the raw alcohol and lets the cook taste it before the stock is committed to an hour of boiling.

questions.q: About how much alcohol remains in a sauce simmered for 15 minutes?
questions.answer: About 40 per cent
questions.why: The USDA's retention table gives about 40 per cent after 15 minutes, 25 per cent after an hour and 5 per cent after two and a half hours; it never reaches none.

questions.q: A finished red wine sauce tastes harsh and raw. What went wrong?
questions.answer: The wine was reduced too little
distractors: Too much butter was mounted in
The shallots were sweated too long
questions.why: Stock and butter soften a raw reduction only a little; the fix is to reduce further, then round it off with stock and a knob of butter.

questions.q: A red wine sauce is bitter and drying. Which wine most likely caused it?
questions.answer: A big, tannic young red, reduced hard
distractors: A light, soft Côtes du Rhône
questions.why: Tannin concentrates as the wine reduces, so a heavily tannic wine reduces to bitterness; a medium-bodied red with moderate tannin is the kitchen's workhorse.

questions.q: Which of these sauces wants dry white wine rather than red?
questions.answer: Beurre blanc
questions.why: White belongs with fish, chicken and the pale sauces; made with red the sauce becomes a different one, beurre rouge, while the three brown preparations stand on red wine.

questions.q: Which two Brennan's preparations are built on red wine?
questions.answer: Marchand de vin and the Owen's short rib braise
distractors: Beurre blanc and the pecan bordelaise
Sauce Foyot and the Creole sauce
questions.why: The marchand de vin and the short rib braise reduce red wine before the stock goes in; the warm emulsions take vinegar or white wine, and the pecan bordelaise is most likely the New Orleans butter kind, confirmed with the kitchen.

questions.q: A guest at breakfast avoids alcohol and asks about the Eggs Owen. What do you say?
questions.answer: It carries wine in the sauce and the braise
distractors: The alcohol has all cooked away
The kitchen uses a bottle with no alcohol
questions.why: The marchand de vin and the short rib braise both carry red wine, and cooking never removes all of it; the honest answer is the plate carries it, then offer another dish.

entries.title: Capers
entries.summary: The unopened flower bud of a Mediterranean shrub, picked by hand and cured in salt or brine until it turns briny, sharp and faintly floral. A small bite that cuts fat, from the tartare dressing to the Grenobloise.
entries.guest: Capers are the cured flower buds of a Mediterranean shrub: small, salty and sharp. On the swordfish they are fried crisp; in the tartare they sit in the dressing with the Dijon.

paras: A caper is the unopened flower bud of Capparis spinosa, a low, scrambling shrub of hot, dry hillsides and old walls around the Mediterranean. The buds are picked by hand before they open, which is why good capers are dear. Fresh, a bud is bitter; curing makes it. Packed in salt or steeped in vinegar brine for weeks, it turns briny, tangy and faintly floral. The caperberry is a different thing: the fruit that forms if the bud is left to flower, picked later on its stem, bigger and milder, served whole like an olive.

Capers are graded by size, and the names are French. Nonpareil, say non-puh-REL, are the smallest, under about 7 mm across, and the dearest; then surfines, capucines, capotes and fines, each a little larger, up to grusas at 14 mm and more. Smaller buds are firmer; larger ones are softer and better for chopping. Salt-packed capers, from Pantelleria and the Aeolian islands off Sicily above all, keep the truest flavour: rinse them, soak them in cold water for 15 to 30 minutes, changing it once, and pat them dry. Brined capers are drained, and rinsed for a dressing.

Fried capers turn a soft, sour pop into crunch. Drain brined capers, or rinse and soak salted ones, then dry them thoroughly on a cloth, because water in hot fat spits. Drop them into neutral oil or clarified butter at about 180°C (356°F), a small handful at a time, and fry for 1 to 2 minutes until they open like tiny flowers, stop bubbling and turn crisp. Lift them onto a rack, never paper, and use them within the hour: they soften as they stand. Frying drives off the water and sharpens the brine into a burst of salt.

Capers earn their place by cutting fat. In the tartare dressing they bring salt and a sharp, briny bite against raw beef and yolk. In the Grenobloise they join brown butter, lemon and parsley over a sautéed fish. In a ravigote they sit with herbs and shallot, and in the French rémoulade with cornichons and herbs in a mayonnaise; each has its own entry. In a piccata they finish a pan sauce of lemon, butter and white wine. Add capers late: long cooking turns them mushy.

Salt-packed capers used unrinsed make a dish too salty to eat, and no lemon rescues it; soak them first and season only after they go in. Capers fried wet spit and never crisp. Fried too long, or in fat that is too hot, they turn dark and bitter. A jar whose buds have gone soft and brown is old: throw it out.

Capers are an old Mediterranean food, salted and pickled around that sea since antiquity, and the plant still grows wild out of the stone of Greek and Roman ruins. In the French kitchen they belong among the sharp garnishes: Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 already sends capers, onion and parsley to the table beside his chopped raw fillet with a yolk, the beefsteak à l'Américaine, an early written ancestor of the steak tartare, which is why caper and tartare still travel together.

At Brennan's the pack places capers on two plates of the Fall 2026 sheet. On the Steak Tartare with Rye they sit inside the tartare dressing with the yolk, Dijon, shallot, hot sauce, parsley and black pepper, the salty, sharp bite that cuts the richness of the yolk; the proportions and the build are the chef's answers. On the Swordfish Grenobloise the capers are fried, the crisp, salty counterpoint to the brown butter and the soft leeks, and part of what makes the garnish Grenobloise rather than a plain meunière. How the kitchen fries them, and in what, is not printed: ask at lineup.

If a guest tastes something briny and bright in the tartare, that is the caper. Describe a fried caper as a caper crisped in hot fat so that it opens and crunches with a burst of salt. A guest who dislikes capers can be told where they are, but whether either plate can be made without them is the kitchen's answer, never a promise at the table.

faults.fix: Soak salted capers first; add the capers, then taste, then salt.

faults.fix: Dry them thoroughly on a cloth before they meet the oil.

Fried until they open and crisp, the capers are the salty crunch against brown butter and soft leek fondue, part of what makes the garnish Grenobloise. How the kitchen fries them, and in what, is a lineup question.

entries.title: Preserved lemon
entries.summary: Lemons packed in salt and their own juice for weeks until the rind turns soft, translucent and perfumed: a North African larder staple a kitchen can make itself, salty and floral rather than sour, and used for its rind.
entries.guest: Preserved lemon is lemon cured in salt for weeks until the peel turns soft and perfumed; it tastes salty and floral rather than sour, and it brightens the butter sauce on the redfish.

paras: A preserved lemon is a whole lemon cut almost through, packed with coarse salt and pressed into a jar with more lemons and their juice, then left for weeks. The salt draws out the juice, the lemons sit under it, and the rind slowly softens and turns translucent while its bitterness mellows into something salty, floral and almost perfumed. It is a staple of the North African larder, of Moroccan tagines above all. The cook uses the rind, rinsed and finely chopped; the pulp is mostly set aside. It is a seasoning, so a dish is salted after it goes in, never before.

Wash unwaxed lemons and cut each from the tip almost to the stem end, in a cross, so it opens but holds together. Pack the cut faces with coarse salt, about 15 g (1 tbsp) a lemon, and press the lemons into a clean jar as tightly as they will go. Cover them with fresh lemon juice until nothing is exposed. Seal the jar and leave it at room temperature for three to four weeks, turning it every few days, until the rind is soft all through. Then keep it in the fridge, where it lasts for months as long as the lemons stay under the juice.

The rind goes where a bright, salty lift is wanted and a squeeze of fresh lemon would thin or curdle the dish. In a beurre blanc it lifts the butter with salt and perfume, where a squeeze of fresh juice at the end would only thin the sauce and taste raw; the reduction already carries the sauce's acid. In an aïoli, say eye-OH-lee, the garlic mayonnaise of Provence, it stands in for part of the lemon juice and adds perfume. A braise of fennel takes a few strips with the olive oil; roasted vegetables take a dressing of chopped rind, oil and herbs. It is at home beside harissa, say huh-REE-suh, the North African chilli paste.

Fresh lemon gives clean, sharp acid from its juice and perfume from its zest, and goes in at the end. Preserved lemon gives salt and perfume with little acid, and it can cook. Lemon confit is an ambiguous name: in French kitchens citron confit most often means this same salt-cured lemon, but it can also mean lemon slices cooked slowly in sugar syrup, which is sweet, so ask which is meant.

The Meyer lemon, thought to be a cross between a lemon and an orange and brought to the United States from China by the plant explorer Frank Meyer in 1908, is sweeter, thinner-skinned and more floral; it makes a gentler preserved lemon that cures faster. Weeks in salt and months in the fridge mean a batch is a lineup question: whether the house cures its own, and what went in.

A batch that grows mould or smells off was not kept under the juice, or the jar was not clean; throw it out, and next time pack tighter and top up with juice. Rind still firm after a month came from thick-skinned fruit or too little salt, and needs more time. A dish gone too salty was seasoned before the lemon, or the rind went in unrinsed. Bitterness comes from the pith of an under-cured lemon, and from the pulp.

At Brennan's the pack places preserved lemon on three plates. On the Redfish Véronique it flavours the beurre blanc, the silky white wine and butter sauce under the redfish, the hibiscus-pickled grapes and the braised leeks. On the Smoked Cauliflower, a dinner side, it partners harissa, salt and perfume against the paste's warmth and the smoke. On the Fish Bouillabaisse of the Fall 2026 sheet it flavours the aïoli beside the fish terrine and the shrimp mousse. Whether the kitchen cures its own and how long the batch has stood are not printed, so confirm them at lineup before you describe it.

Describe it to a guest as lemon cured in salt, salty and perfumed rather than sour, with the peel eaten and the flesh set aside. On the Véronique it makes the butter sauce bright without making it sharp; on the cauliflower it answers the harissa. The curing takes weeks, so whether the house cures its own and what went into the batch are the kitchen's answers.

ratios.label: Salt for each lemon
ratios.value: About 15 g (1 tbsp) of coarse salt, pressed into the cut faces, plus a spoonful on top

ratios.label: The cure
ratios.value: Three to four weeks at room temperature, under the juice, the jar turned every few days

ratios.label: Keeping
ratios.value: Months in the fridge, as long as the lemons stay under the juice

faults.fault: Mould, or a jar that smells off
faults.cause: The lemons were not kept under the juice, or the jar was not clean.
faults.fix: Throw it out; pack the next batch tighter and top it up with fresh lemon juice.

faults.fault: Rind still firm after a month
faults.cause: Thick-skinned fruit, or too little salt.
faults.fix: Give it more time; use thinner-skinned lemons and the full measure of salt next time.

faults.cause: Seasoned before the preserved lemon went in, or the rind unrinsed.
faults.fix: Rinse the rind; add it, taste, then salt.

faults.cause: Pith from an under-cured lemon, or pulp left in.
faults.fix: Use only the soft rind of a fully cured lemon and set the pulp aside.

brennans.how: Chopped preserved lemon flavours the beurre blanc under the redfish, lifting the butter sauce with salt and perfume rather than sharp acid, beside the hibiscus-pickled grapes and braised leeks.
On the smoked cauliflower the preserved lemon partners harissa: salt and perfume against the chilli paste's warmth and the smoke. The harissa brings moderate heat, so warn a spice-shy guest.

Preserved lemon flavours the aïoli, the garlic sauce of Provence, beside the fish terrine, shrimp mousse and bouillabaisse sauce. The sheet names an aioli, not rouille, so say aioli; what is in tonight's batch is the kitchen's answer.

entries.title: Beef tenderloin and the Chateaubriand
entries.say: As it reads: beef tenderloin; Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN.
entries.summary: The tenderloin is the long, lean muscle along the inside of the backbone that does almost no work, so it is the most tender cut and the mildest. The filet mignon, the Chateaubriand and the steak tartare are all cut from it.
entries.guest: The Chateaubriand is the thick centre of the tenderloin, the most tender cut, roasted whole for two to the temperature you choose and carved; lean, so at its best pink, with a rich sauce.

paras: The tenderloin is the long, tapering muscle that lies along the inside of the backbone. It does almost no work, so its fibres stay fine and it carries little connective tissue, the most tender cut on the animal. It is also lean: tenderness and marbling are different things, and the tenderloin has the first without much of the second, so its flavour is mild and it leans on its crust and its sauce.

A whole tenderloin comes in three parts. The head is the thick end. The centre cut is the even cylinder in the middle, and that is the Chateaubriand, say shah-toh-bree-AHN, the roast for two. The tail is thin, best for tartare or medallions. The chain, a sinewy strip along one side, is pulled away for stock, and the silverskin, a pearly membrane that never melts in cooking, is sliced off with the tip of a thin knife held flat.

USDA Prime is the most marbled beef from young cattle, Choice the broad middle, Select the leanest; the grade is a quality stamp, not a cut. Creekstone Farms, the Black Angus producer named on the Roasted Chateaubriand and the hanger steaks, grades Prime and Choice, so say Prime only where the menu prints it.

A thick centre cut is cooked like a small roast. Trim it, tie it so it keeps an even shape, and salt it. Sear it hard on every side to a deep brown crust, then move it to an oven at about 200°C (392°F) and roast it until the centre reaches the temperature the guest asked for; a 700 g (1.5 lb) Chateaubriand takes roughly 15 to 25 minutes to medium-rare.
Pull it early, because the centre keeps rising as it rests. Rest it on a board for about ten minutes, then carve thick slices across the grain, so every slice has a crust and a pink heart.

The filet mignon is a thick steak cut across the tenderloin, 170 to 225 g (6 to 8 oz). A Chateaubriand is the centre cut roasted whole for two. Served raw, the tenderloin becomes steak tartare, say tar-TAR: trimmed of every sinew, cut by hand, never minced in a machine, which turns it pasty and grey, and dressed at the last moment with yolk, mustard, capers and shallot. Because it is raw, the consumer advisory is given before the order is taken.

A grey band under the crust and a dry centre: roasted too hot for too long, or not rested; pull it earlier and rest it. No crust: the meat was wet or the pan not hot enough. A chewy, grey tartare: minced by machine or cut hours ahead; cut it by hand, cold, to order.

The name Chateaubriand is said to come from Montmireil, chef to the writer François-René de Chateaubriand, who around 1822 roasted the thick cut between two lesser steaks that were thrown away; by Escoffier's Guide of 1903 the Chateaubriand is simply a thick cut from the centre of the fillet, grilled for two. The tartare has an ancestor rather than an inventor: Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire of 1903 records beefsteak à l'Américaine, chopped raw fillet with a yolk, capers, onion and parsley beside it.

At Brennan's the pack carries the tenderloin on four plates. The Roasted Chateaubriand is Creekstone Farms tenderloin roasted whole for two at $120, with glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot; ask the temperature once for the table. The Chateau Espagnole on the Fall 2026 sheet is a 340 g (12 oz) centre cut with frascarelli and sauce Espagnole: no price, method, serving count or producer is printed, so promise none. The Steak Tartare with Rye is raw tenderloin, chopped and dressed. The Petite Filet Mignon is the fourth course of the Traditional Breakfast.

Say Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, and tartare, tar-TAR. Describe the tenderloin as the most tender cut and a lean one, served pink because it has little fat to carry it further. Take the temperature with the order, repeat it back and write it down; a whole roast takes longer than a steak, so say so. For the tartare, say raw before anything else and give the consumer advisory; questions about the egg yolk, the portion or the beef's source go to the kitchen.
